does: Adds sugar to a food a little at a time and tastes after each addition, to bring it to the right level of sweetness without hiding its own taste.

intro.what: Sweetening adds sugar gradually until it balances rather than hides the food’s own taste.
intro.why: It teaches you to dissolve additions fully and judge the result before adding more.

how: Cook the food until it is soft enough to take up the sugar.
Add the sugar in portions, stirring each in until it has dissolved.
Taste after each portion and stop when the sweetness is balanced.
Add a small amount of salt at the end to round the taste.

cues.text: The sweetness is clear but does not drown the taste of the food.

mistakes.mistake: Adding all the sugar at once, so that it is too sweet and cannot be corrected.
mistakes.fix: Add it a little at a time.

mistakes.mistake: Adding sugar to dried beans before they are soft, so that they stay hard.

quiz.question: What should balanced sweetness preserve?
choices: The flavour of the food beneath the sugar.
A gritty layer of undissolved sugar.
quiz.because: Sweetness should support the ingredient rather than overwhelm its character.

quiz.question: When should the next sugar addition be judged?
choices: Before the previous sugar has dissolved.
After stirring the previous addition until dissolved and tasting.
Only after adding all the sugar available.
quiz.because: Dissolving distributes sweetness so tasting can guide the next addition accurately.

quiz.question: Which appearance indicates the sugar has dissolved?
choices: A pile of crystals sits at the base.
quiz.because: Sugar needs to dissolve into the food rather than remain as separate gritty crystals.

quiz.question: A batch becomes overwhelmingly sweet. What should change next time?
choices: Add sugar gradually and taste between additions.
Add the entire amount before tasting.
Judge the sweetness before the previous addition has dissolved.
quiz.because: Small additions let you stop before sweetness masks the food.
